analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil and gas windfall profits to fund transit fare cuts and fuel-efficient car credits.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referrals and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed an excise tax on oil and natural gas company profits above a level a new federal board deemed reasonable, taxing the excess at 50% to 100%. It would have used that revenue for two things aimed at people squeezed by gas prices: grants to bus and commuter rail systems to cut fares, and tax credits of $3,000 to $6,000 for buying highly fuel-efficient cars built in the United States by unionized workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Commuters and drivers facing gas price spikes, through cheaper bus and rail fares and credits toward fuel-efficient vehicles; unionized U.S. auto plants whose vehicles would qualify for the credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, transit riders, and unionized autoworkers

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on oil and gas sales, taking 50% of profit up to 2% above a board-set 'reasonable profit,' 75% up to 5% above, and 100% of anything beyond that [S2, S3].

Allows individual buyers a tax credit of $3,000, $4,500, or $6,000 for a fuel-efficient passenger vehicle assembled in the U.S. by workers under a collective bargaining agreement, with the top credit for cars rated at least 65 mpg [S2, S3].

Authorizes the Transportation Secretary to grant mass transit systems — buses and commuter rail — money to reduce fares for all riders, funded by whatever the windfall tax collects beyond the cost of the car credits [S2, S3].
Creates a three-member Reasonable Profits Board, appointed by the President, whose members may hold no financial interest in the oil and gas businesses they assess [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas companies and their shareholders, who would owe the excise tax on profits deemed excessive; some of the cost could surface at the pump to the extent producers adjust prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: 'Reasonable profit' is a vague standard set by a small appointed board, giving that board sweeping discretion over one of the economy's largest industries — an approach critics of past windfall profit taxes said invites arbitrary decisions and litigation (general explanation of the mechanism; not in the sources).

A windfall profits tax can reduce oil companies' incentive to invest in domestic production; the 1970s-era federal windfall profits tax is widely cited by economists for collecting far less revenue than projected (general explanation of the mechanism; not in the sources).

The car credit is limited to vehicles built in the U.S. under collective bargaining agreements, excluding cheaper or more fuel-efficient models built by non-union or foreign-owned plants, so the consumer benefit is narrower than a simple fuel-economy credit would be [S3].
The transit fare-reduction fund is only as large as the windfall tax revenue left over after paying for the car credits, so if the tax underperforms, the fare relief does too [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-facing benefits — cheaper fares during price spikes and credits for efficient cars — are real and would be paid for mostly by oil company profits rather than by ordinary taxpayers. The design flaws are the vague 'reasonable profit' standard, which concentrates a lot of discretionary pricing power in a three-member board, and the union-only restriction on the car credit, which narrows who can actually claim it. On balance the bill transfers money from a concentrated industry to drivers and transit riders, but its administrative machinery is crude by the standards of a well-designed tax.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Transportation committees, sent to a highways subcommittee, and then nothing happened; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever came, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Kucinich and five Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on January 18, 2012 [S1, S3].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S5].
One day later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
Neither committee took it up, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept all their profits from the 2012 price run-up untaxed by any windfall levy, and no new board ever reviewed them; drivers and transit riders received no relief. The bill's six House sponsors gained only the record of having introduced it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and their shareholders

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; all six of its sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican ever signed on [S3, S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would tax 50% to 100% of their profits above a board-determined 'reasonable profit' on every sale of crude oil, natural gas, and fuels made from them. High pump prices were the occasion for the bill, so the industry's interest in untaxed profits ran directly against consumers during price spikes.

The $3,000–$6,000 purchase credit applies only to fuel-efficient cars assembled in the United States by workers under a collective bargaining agreement, steering buyers toward unionized domestic plants. Non-union and foreign-owned assembly plants are excluded from the benefit.

Bus and commuter rail systems would receive federal grants to cut fares for all riders during gas price spikes, with funding drawn from the windfall tax revenue. Cheaper fares would pull some riders off the road when driving is most expensive.
